At the small school in Kumarakom, Francis noticed it in pieces. First Ankita stopped coming to the tea shop after class. Then her lunch box went home full, three days running. On Thursday, when he asked about the district quiz they had trained for all year, she shrugged. “Doesn't matter. Nothing really matters.”
He walked home along the canal, turning it over. Maybe she's just tired, he thought. Everyone has bad weeks. But it wasn't one thing. It was the quiz, the lunch, the tea shop, and now those words. Waiting to see felt like the easy choice, not the right one. If I'm wrong, I'm embarrassed. If I'm right and I wait, that's worse.
He turned round and went back. Mrs Mathew, their class teacher, was still marking in the staffroom. He told her everything, word for word. She thanked him, called Ankita's mother while he was still there and asked her to stay close to Ankita that evening, and said she and the school counsellor would sit with Ankita first thing.

Behind the panchayat school in their village near Madurai, Keerthana sat on the low wall and didn't open her tiffin. Vandana sat down beside her and didn't open hers either.
“You don't have to talk,” Vandana said. After a while: “But how are you really? Not the fine version.”
Keerthana's eyes filled. It came out slowly: her father's shop closing, the shouting at home, feeling like a weight on everyone. Vandana didn't say cheer up, or that others have it worse. She just listened, nodding, and once said, “That sounds so heavy.”
When Keerthana finished, Vandana said, “You matter to me. A lot. And I'm not a counsellor; I don't know how to fix this. Can we go to Selvi Teacher together, now?”
Keerthana hesitated, then nodded. Selvi Teacher closed the staffroom door and listened, and that afternoon she walked home with Keerthana to speak to her mother.

After netball practice in Leeds, Chidi found Freya sitting on the floor of the changing room long after everyone had gone, knees pulled up. Chidi sat down next to her, not too close.
“I'm not going to lecture you,” Chidi said. “I just want to know how you're actually doing.”
Freya picked at her laces. “Bad. Since Mum left, home is so quiet. Sometimes I think nobody would notice if I disappeared.”
Chidi felt her stomach drop, but kept her voice steady. “I'd notice. You matter, Freya. To me, and to loads of people.” She stayed where she was. She didn't try to argue Freya out of feeling sad.
“I don't know how to help with the big stuff,” Chidi said. “But Mrs Okafor's still in the PE office. Will you come with me? I'll stay.”
They went together. Mrs Okafor listened, then called Freya's dad and the school's safeguarding lead before either girl left the building.

Dear Chetan Bhaiya,
You said to plan before I talk to Sonal, so I've written it out. Please tell me if it sounds okay.
Where: after school, on the bench behind the canteen, just the two of us.
What I'll say first: “I've noticed you seem really low lately, and I'm worried about you. I care about you.”
Then I stop talking and let her answer, even if the silence is long.
If she gets angry and says I'm being nosy: “Okay. I'm not trying to push. I'm still here whenever you want.” And I'll try again another day.
If she shuts down and won't talk: I'll tell Ms Fernandes, our class teacher, the same day, because it's too important to wait.
If she says anything about hurting herself: I stay with her and get Ms Fernandes or another adult straight away.
I'm nervous. But having it written down helps.
Madhuri
